title: Percy's Pigeon Problem
markdown:
The Whispering Page was a bookshop so crammed with stories it seemed to exhale them. It sat on a cobbled lane in a smell of old paper, dust that had read itself, and other people's adventures. Morning light came in stripes between the shelves. Percy ran it: a charcoal-grey cat organized to the last whisker, a purring archivist who dusted spines, aligned bookmarks by height, and offered a quiet shush to any page that fluttered without an appointment. Customers left calmer than they arrived. The shop preferred it that way.

His allotment was another country. Colour rioted. Bees tumbled from lavender, round as teacups. Mrs. Higgins waved from pumpkins already the size of armchairs. Young Timmy ran a snail ranch that consisted mostly of watching a bucket. Seeds, Percy felt, had a rebellious streak. Sunflowers loomed where he had planned carrots. Nasturtiums twined his radishes with brassy confidence.

"It's anarchy," he would murmur, tail ticking.

Bram the weasel was the opposite of a catalogue. His laugh sounded like wind chimes that had somewhere to be. His tail investigated first and explained later. He found Percy's fussiness baffling and, worse, charming.

"But Percy," Bram would say, eyes bright, "that's the fun. A little wildness. Imagine if every story in your shop were the same story, perfectly, predictably."

He brought stray feathers and interesting pebbles. Percy sighed and found each a very specific shelf.

Percy, however, had a plan. He had lists: Seeds That Behave, Seeds That Wander, Seeds Requiring Gentle Persuasion. Soil preferences wore tiny coloured markers. His hypothesis, entirely his own, was that if you clearly marked where things should not be, the world would take the hint.

"The best ideas, though odd, often sprout from careful observation," he told Bram, spectacles sliding. Bram had berry juice on his chin. "And a clear sign, of course."

He painted the sign in block letters, with a stern carrot whose leafy top bristled. STRICTLY NO STRAY SEED ZONE. OFFENDERS WILL BE REMOVED. EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY. A small diagram showed an offended sunflower being escorted away by two prim daisies. Percy considered it a masterpiece of declarative gardening.

He marched to the allotment. Bram trotted behind, sniffing roots, briefly employed in beetle-chase. Percy chose a sun patch near his most silk-flag seedlings and hammered the sign home. It stood proud against the unruly green.

"There," he purred, a rare smile, tail content. "Let the seeds know their place."

Bram chatted with Mrs. Higgins about giant pumpkins. He admired Timmy's ranch. He offered a critique of an over-enthusiastic runner bean. He looked at Percy's sign with a twinkle that suggested the green had not finished speaking.

Pigeons have opinions. Percy's official letters and comical carrot read, to pigeon minds, as a flashing invitation. STRAY SEED ZONE became Free Buffet. Official Dining Hall. All Welcome.

Wings. The thump of landings. The sharp scent of birdseed gone sociable. They did not parse "offenders will be removed." They parsed food. A first pigeon arrived with the confidence of a regular. A second brought friends. Then the air was mostly pigeons. They pecked the lettering, mistaking crisp paint for crumbs. They waddled until the sign leaned, then lay down, official side in the dirt. Percy's prize pumpkin became a landing strip, then a conversation pit. His radish rows acquired what gardeners call evidence of avian appreciation, plus a few sunflower seeds carried in as souvenirs. A lettuce, which had been minding its manners, vanished under a committee.

Percy's fur stood. His catalogued afternoon came apart. A tremor ran his whiskers. Bram watched with delight. One plump bird strutted the fallen board as if newly appointed Head of Pigeon Affairs.

"Oh, Percy," Bram chuckled, dry leaves on a path, "I think your sign is a little too inviting. More welcome, feathered friends, than strictly no."

Percy slumped onto a patch of mint that had never applied for permission. The scent was sharp and clean and did nothing useful for dignity. His lists felt like scribbles. The pigeons cooed, professionally oblivious. Mrs. Higgins peered over, tying a runner bean, voice warm.

"Having a bit of trouble with your no-fly zone, Percy?"

He sat. For a breath that was not a lecture, he only sat. Mint under charcoal fur. Sun on the fallen sign. A pigeon, quite close, turned a seed with one pink foot as if considering a library fine.

Then he saw it: where the chaotic pecking had scattered what they had not swallowed, tiny sprouts were already shouldering up, eager and unlisted.

Bram nudged him. "Look. Even their mess is making new things. Unintentional sowing."

He grabbed a watering can and began, with surprising energy, to tidy: feathers scooped, seedlings eased back, water for the ones that had just arrived. Other allotment holders ambled over. Timmy offered interestingly shaped pebbles to weigh the sign, decorative in his view. Mrs. Higgins, with a wink, brought bread crusts and redirected the buffet toward a less horticultural corner.

The plot was no longer Percy's solitary ordered domain. It was a slightly messy, thoroughly alive place where neighbours arrived without being catalogued first. Percy watched Bram shoo a last enthusiast from the lettuce with a bright scarf, and a different satisfaction arrived, warmer than any prize pumpkin.

He still loved lists. He added a heading: Unexpected Benefactors (Feathered Division). The sign, battered, printed with pigeon feet, became less a warning than a landmark. The birds, well fed and occasionally amused by the spectacled gardener who re-alphabetized fallen seeds, stayed part of the noise.

On a bench that leaned as if it, too, had opinions, Percy and Bram shared chamomile from a flask that had never been labeled, which Percy decided not to mention. Colour kept rioting. Bees went on with the lavender as if no decree had been issued. The stern carrot on the sign now wore a dusty toe-print, which rather improved it. Percy, sipping, did not straighten the bench. The tea steamed, apple-faint and ordinary. A pigeon considered them, decided against, and went to sit on the word ZONE as if it had always been a cushion. From the lane, the bookshop would be exhaling its quiet paper breath. Here the air was mint and feathers and a list that had learned a new heading. Percy left both as they were.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
